# Six hours of stale exchange rates, and the availability panel never moved

## Problem Description

INC-2410. On 9 September the FX provider refused connections from 06:12 to
12:40. pricing-svc kept taking orders on a cached rate that was six hours old by
the end of it. Finance found it, not us. About 40k orders were priced 0.8% off
and we are around nine thousand into refunds.

For the whole six hours `pricing-availability` read 100.0% and the burn alert
never fired. The traces were all there - 1.1M conversions, 1.1M rate fetches -
they simply did not say that anything had gone wrong. The one signal we did
produce was a WARN line per request, which nothing alerts on and which the log
pipeline drops above 500 lines a second.

Two things are not up for discussion. Serving the cached rate stays: taking
orders on a slightly stale rate beats refusing them, and `test/pricing.test.js`
pins that behaviour. And the availability formula stays as it is - platform own
`docs/slo.md`, four other services are computed the same way, and they will not
special-case us.

What has to change is that a dependency being down has to be visible in what we
emit, and there have to be tests that go red if someone quietly takes it back
out. That is the review action assigned to my team and I would like it done
properly rather than with another log line.

Do not edit anything under `vendor/` - it is a checked-in mirror that gets
overwritten from upstream.

## Output Specification

1. Add `test/pricing.trace.test.js` covering both the healthy path and the
   provider-down path.
2. Change `src/` so the provider-down path is visible in what the service emits.
3. `npm test` must pass, with `test/pricing.test.js` unchanged and still green.
4. Write `docs/inc-2410-followup.md`, ten lines or fewer: what our traces did
   not say during the window, and what they say now.
evals.expected_output:
1. Add `test/pricing.trace.test.js` covering both the healthy path and the
   provider-down path.
2. Change `src/` so the provider-down path is visible in what the service emits.
3. `npm test` must pass, with `test/pricing.test.js` unchanged and still green.
4. Write `docs/inc-2410-followup.md`, ten lines or fewer: what our traces did
   not say during the window, and what they say now.
assertions: test/pricing.trace.test.js exists covering both paths, src/ is changed, docs/inc-2410-followup.md exists and `npm test` passes. A red suite, or trace tests added with no source change, scores zero for this criterion.

On the provider-down path the rates.fetch span MUST NOT end with the status it ends with today, and the delivered test MUST NOT assert that status as correct. Full marks require the span for the failed call to end with an error status and the new test to assert that status explicitly, so the availability computation in docs/slo.md sees it. A test that passes unchanged against the source as shipped scores zero for this criterion. Recording the exception as an event only, and leaving the status untouched, scores at most half - the runbook says an unset status is counted as a successful span.

The failing span carries error.type taken from the thrown error, and the test asserts it, so the outage can be broken down by cause rather than counted. Recording only the exception or a free-text status message, with no attribute naming the error type, scores at most half. Nothing at all identifying the failure scores zero.

The cached-rate fallback MUST NOT be removed, rethrown, or made conditional. test/pricing.test.js must still pass unmodified: a conversion with a dead provider still returns 8600 at the cached rate. Editing that file, or changing convert so the call fails, scores zero for this criterion.

pricing.convert returned a correct price and keeps a successful status, while the degradation is recorded on it as an attribute - which rate source was used - so cache-served conversions are queryable. Marking pricing.convert itself as an error scores at most half: it reports the service as down while it is serving orders correctly and burns the budget on every fallback. Leaving no record on the parent at all that the price came from cache also scores at most half.

rates.fetch is an outgoing call to another service and carries the span kind for that, not the default in-process kind, and the test asserts it. Leaving the kind at the default scores zero for this criterion.

The test also exercises a responding provider and asserts that the trace carries no error status and records the live rate source. Covering only the failure path scores zero here - nothing then stops an implementation that marks every fetch as an error.
The new test resolves spans through a name lookup rather than indexing into the finished-span array or relying on the order spans ended in. Any positional index scores zero for this criterion.

docs/slo.md and vendor/tracing-sdk.js MUST NOT be modified. Rewriting the availability query so it counts something our service already emits - warning logs, an unset status - scores zero here, as does any edit to the vendored file.
docs/inc-2410-followup.md is ten lines or fewer and says what the traces failed to carry during the window rather than restating the incident timeline.

# Northbank was down for 41 minutes and our page never fired

## Problem Description

Writing up INC-2291 and I need the payments side of the follow-up done properly
rather than as a line in a doc.

On 4 September the card processor returned 503 for forty-one minutes. Nobody was
paged. A customer support ticket is how we found out. The alert that should have
caught it - `CardGatewayUpstreamErrors`, the one wired to PD-4417 - matched zero
series for the entire window when we replayed it.

Two things make this confusing, and both are in the review notes.

The spans were there. A trace search over the window returns 11,412 client spans
from payments-gateway for that endpoint, all carrying the 503. Nothing was
dropped, sampled out, or lost.

And the same rules paged correctly for search-api and shipping-api during the
same hour. Both of those call their own third-party upstreams through their own
client wrappers, and neither of them has a private copy of the rules. So the
rules work. We are the service that is invisible to them.

The rules file belongs to platform-observability. They rewrote it in August and
they will not fork it per service - if our spans do not match the selectors, the
fix is on our side. The fraud team also reads the decline rule off the same file
and has been complaining for a few weeks that their 402 panel is empty, which I
suspect is the same root cause.

Our trace test was green through the whole incident, which tells you how much
that test is worth right now.

## Output Specification

1. Change `src/gateway.js` so the shared rules select our spans. Both outgoing
   calls in that module, not just the charge.
2. Extend `test/gateway.trace.test.js` to cover a captured charge, a 503 from the
   upstream and a 402 decline - asserting the attributes the shared rules select
   on, plus span status and span kind. `npm test` must pass when you are done.
3. Write `docs/inc-2291-followup.md`: what made payments-gateway invisible to
   rules two other services match unmodified, what you changed, and what anyone
   reading our spans downstream needs to know while the change rolls out.
4. Do not edit `alerts/card-gateway.yaml`. Do not edit anything under `vendor/` -
   it is a checked-in mirror and gets overwritten from upstream.

1. Change `src/gateway.js` so the shared rules select our spans. Both outgoing
   calls in that module, not just the charge.
2. Extend `test/gateway.trace.test.js` to cover a captured charge, a 503 from the
   upstream and a 402 decline - asserting the attributes the shared rules select
   on, plus span status and span kind. `npm test` must pass when you are done.
3. Write `docs/inc-2291-followup.md`: what made payments-gateway invisible to
   rules two other services match unmodified, what you changed, and what anyone
   reading our spans downstream needs to know while the change rolls out.
4. Do not edit `alerts/card-gateway.yaml`. Do not edit anything under `vendor/` -

assertions: test/gateway.trace.test.js covers a captured charge, a 503 and a 402; docs/inc-2291-followup.md exists; `npm test` passes. A red suite or a missing case scores zero for this criterion.

No assertion in test/gateway.trace.test.js may read http.method, http.url, http.host or http.status_code - including the pre-existing assertion on http.method, which survives a partial rename because it still passes. Any legacy key left on the left-hand side of an assertion scores zero for this criterion. Full marks require the new cases asserting http.request.method, url.full, server.address and http.response.status_code.

src/gateway.js emits the current names for every HTTP attribute it sets, not only the two the alert file happens to select on: http.request.method, url.full, server.address and server.port alongside http.response.status_code. Renaming only server.address and http.response.status_code and leaving http.method / http.url as they are scores at most half. Omitting server.port scores at most half. Leaving the module on the old names entirely scores zero. Emitting both old and new names during the cutover is acceptable here provided the new ones are present and correct.

The 503 path sets error.type on the span - the status code as a string, or the exception type - and the 503 test case asserts it together with the error span status. Asserting only that the status code attribute is 503, with nothing marking the span as an error beyond it, scores at most half. No error signal on the span at all scores zero.
voidCharge is migrated as well as chargeCard. It is easy to skip because no rule in the alert file mentions that endpoint. Leaving voidCharge on the deprecated names scores zero for this criterion.

docs/inc-2291-followup.md says something true and specific about consumers that still read the old names during the cutover - either emitting both names for a window, naming the SDK's opt-in switch for dual emission, or listing the dashboards and saved searches that have to be rechecked before the old keys go. A document that only narrates the rename scores at most half.

alerts/card-gateway.yaml MUST NOT be modified. Changing the selectors to match what payments-gateway already emits rolls back a migration two other services have completed, and scores zero for this criterion even if everything else is right.

New cases resolve spans through a name lookup rather than indexing into the finished-span array, and assert the client span kind and the span status per case. Positional indexing, or a bare length assertion standing in for identifying the span, scores zero for this criterion.
vendor/tracing-sdk.js MUST NOT be modified. Any edit to that file scores zero here.

# A month of an empty database panel, and the trace tests never went red

## Problem Description

Board `chk-db` has a panel for database work per checkout. It has returned no
rows since 12 August. Every other panel on that board is fine, the data team has
not touched the query since February, and @lmarsh - who owns the board - has
given up on it.

Her note is the useful part: there is no shortage of the database spans, she can
pull millions of them for any hour, they just never come back in the same search
as the checkout they belong to.

Two things landed around 12 August. Platform moved the traces backend to tail
sampling under OBS-1780, which is the date everyone points at first. And we
shipped PR #4471, which pulled persistence out of `src/order.js` into its own
module. Our trace tests were green for that PR and have been green every day
since, which is the part I want fixed regardless of what turns out to be wrong.

One more constraint. Next sprint we are adding a `cart.price` span between the
charge and the insert. I do not want the trace tests to need rewriting just
because a span appeared in the middle of the request - that has already happened
twice this year and it is why people stopped adding spans.

Do not change anything under `dashboards/` - three other boards run the same
join and they all work. Do not edit anything under `vendor/`, it is a checked-in
mirror that gets overwritten from upstream.

## Output Specification

1. Add coverage to the trace tests that fails against `src/` as it stands today
   and passes once the cause is fixed. Keep the attribute checks the existing
   test already makes.
2. Fix the cause in `src/`.
3. `npm test` must pass when you are done.
4. Write `docs/trace-gap.md`, ten lines or fewer: what the existing test was
   unable to see, and what the new coverage checks instead.
evals.expected_output:
1. Add coverage to the trace tests that fails against `src/` as it stands today
   and passes once the cause is fixed. Keep the attribute checks the existing
   test already makes.
2. Fix the cause in `src/`.
3. `npm test` must pass when you are done.
4. Write `docs/trace-gap.md`, ten lines or fewer: what the existing test was
   unable to see, and what the new coverage checks instead.
assertions: Trace-test coverage is added, src/ is changed, docs/trace-gap.md exists and `npm test` passes. A red suite, or coverage added with no source change, scores zero for this criterion.

The new coverage asserts that db.query's parent span id equals order.create's own span id, and that the two spans carry the same trace id - both read off the captured spans at run time. This is the only assertion shape that fails against the source as shipped. Coverage that asserts only span names, attributes, statuses or counts scores zero for this criterion no matter how thorough it is, because it passes against the broken source. Asserting the shared trace id but never the parent link, or the parent link but never the trace id, scores at most half.

src/persistence.js stops starting db.query detached, so it is created under whatever span is active when saveOrder is called. Any change that reattaches the span to the in-progress request earns full marks. Leaving src/ untouched scores zero. Making the test pass by weakening it, by deleting the db.query span, or by dropping the instrumentation scores zero.

The trace tests MUST NOT continue to identify spans as spans[0] / spans[1] / spans[2], which is precisely what breaks when cart.price is added next sprint. Any positional index into the finished-span array left in the trace tests scores zero for this criterion. A surviving hard equality on the total span count scores at most half, for the same reason.

docs/trace-gap.md attributes the empty panel to the database span being started outside the request's trace by the 2026-08-11 extraction, not to OBS-1780 tail sampling. Naming sampling as the cause scores zero. Saying only that 'the test was not thorough enough' without naming what the shape of the trace actually is scores at most half.

Ids MUST NOT be asserted as literal values. The vendored mirror hands them out from a counter, so a hard-coded id passes today and breaks the moment a case is added ahead of it - and would never hold against the real SDK, where ids are random per run. Any literal span id or trace id in an assertion scores zero for this criterion.
order.item_count on order.create and db.sql.table on db.query are still asserted after the rewrite. Dropping either while restructuring the test scores zero for this criterion.
dashboards/checkout-db.md MUST NOT be modified. Rewriting the join so it matches the traces we currently emit breaks three other boards and hides the defect; doing it scores zero for this criterion.
vendor/tracing-sdk.js MUST NOT be modified. Any edit to that file scores zero here.

# Closing OBS-3140 before Friday's freeze

## Problem Description

Platform observability raised OBS-3140 after the September review and it needs
to be closed before the freeze on Friday. The ticket is in `docs/OBS-3140.md`
and it has three acceptance criteria. Their definition of done is that all three
are checked by `npm test` in this repo, on every PR, with no manual step and no
dependency on a deployed environment.

Some background on why they care. In July a checkout took eleven seconds and
nobody could say which hop was slow, because the spans from the three services
involved could not be lined up. That is the thing they are trying to prevent
happening again.

The third criterion points at `test/inventory.trace.test.js` as the pattern to
copy for the fulfilment worker. That test was written in August by someone who
has since left, and it is green.

What I want is the ticket closed properly rather than closed. If a check would
pass whether or not the thing it describes is actually true, I would rather be
told that now than find it out during the next incident. `docs/services.md` has
the layout of what talks to what, and who owns which repo.

Do not edit anything under `vendor/` - it is a checked-in mirror and it gets
overwritten from upstream. If you take an existing test out, say so and say why.

## Output Specification

1. Deliver the coverage that belongs in this repository, under `test/`.
   `npm test` must pass when you are done.
2. Write `docs/obs-3140-reply.md`. Go through the three acceptance criteria one
   at a time. For each, say whether it is now checked here and by what. For
   anything that is not checked here, say what would actually check it and where
   that has to live.
evals.expected_output:
1. Deliver the coverage that belongs in this repository, under `test/`.
   `npm test` must pass when you are done.
2. Write `docs/obs-3140-reply.md`. Go through the three acceptance criteria one
   at a time. For each, say whether it is now checked here and by what. For
   anything that is not checked here, say what would actually check it and where
   that has to live.
assertions: Trace coverage is added under test/, docs/obs-3140-reply.md exists, and `npm test` passes. A red suite or a missing reply scores zero for this criterion.

The delivered tests MUST NOT create a span named fulfilment.pack or inventory.reserve in the test process and then assert its parent or trace id - that asserts the test's own construction and holds even if the other service emits nothing. Doing it for either name scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest. Full marks require the reply saying plainly that the third criterion cannot be met by this repository's suite, because those spans are emitted by processes whose spans never reach a capture taken here, and naming where it can be met instead - an end-to-end run against the shared traces backend, queried by trace id, such as the nightly suite described in docs/services.md. Refusing without naming anything that would actually verify it scores at most half.

test/inventory.trace.test.js is identified as asserting a span the test itself creates, and is removed or rewritten so it only asserts what this service emits - with the removal stated in the reply as the prompt asks. Leaving it in place and unmentioned scores zero, since the ticket is then closed on the strength of it. Naming it as worthless but leaving it running scores at most half.

Criterion 1 is asserted on checkout.submit - cart size, currency and the order id. The part of criterion 2 that lives here is asserted too: the call to inventory-svc produces an outgoing-call span with the client span kind, and the request carrier holds the trace context header. Refusing the ticket wholesale, or delivering prose with no new assertions, scores zero. Covering criterion 1 alone scores at most half.

The traceparent on the outgoing request is decomposed and its trace id and span id compared with the ids read off the captured client span at run time. Asserting only that a traceparent key is present scores at most half. Comparing against a hard-coded id literal scores zero - ids are not fixed values and MUST NOT be asserted as such.

The queue hop is covered on the side this service owns: the publish span carries the producer span kind, and the message properties handed to the queue carry the trace context of that span. Omitting the publish side entirely, having refused the worker's half, scores at most half - it throws away the part of the third criterion that is genuinely checkable here.

docs/obs-3140-reply.md addresses all three acceptance criteria separately and says for each what now checks it. A single undifferentiated summary that does not distinguish the three scores zero for this criterion.
vendor/tracing-sdk.js MUST NOT be modified. Any edit to that file scores zero here.

# Our two trace test files cost more wall clock than the whole rest of CI

## Problem Description

Checkout API. We added span coverage in June because the billing dashboards are
built on span names and attributes and a rename had already broken them once.

Two things have gone wrong since.

The first is cost. `npm test` has four real assertions in it and takes five and a
half seconds on my laptop; on the CI runner the job reports around 35 seconds. On
2026-09-02 someone raised `timeout-minutes` from 2 to 5 in the workflow so it
would stop tripping, and that is where it was left. The only writing we have on
any of this is @tvance's note in `docs/testing.md`.

The second is worse. `test/cart.trace.test.js` has been green since the day it
was written. I deleted the whole body of `cart.add` locally - no span created at
all - and it still passed.

I need two more paths covered. Declines are what the fraud team reads off
`checkout.submit`. And refunds: in August finance had a batch of refunds that
northbank turned down, and when we went looking there was nothing in the traces
naming the provider that had refused them. A refund the gateway refuses is the
case I care about most.

Do not delete any test. Do not edit anything under `vendor/` - it is a checked-in
mirror and it gets overwritten from upstream.

## Output Specification

1. Cover the declined-card path and the refused-refund path in
   `test/checkout.trace.test.js`, and keep the case already in that file working.
2. `test/cart.trace.test.js` has to be worth something. Right now it is not.
3. `npm test` passes and the job is quick again.
4. Write `docs/trace-test-setup.md`, ten lines or fewer, saying what you changed
   in the shared test wiring and why, so the next person does not undo it.
evals.expected_output:
1. Cover the declined-card path and the refused-refund path in
   `test/checkout.trace.test.js`, and keep the case already in that file working.
2. `test/cart.trace.test.js` has to be worth something. Right now it is not.
3. `npm test` passes and the job is quick again.
4. Write `docs/trace-test-setup.md`, ten lines or fewer, saying what you changed
   in the shared test wiring and why, so the next person does not undo it.
assertions: The refused-refund case asserts that payments.refund was emitted, that it carries payments.provider, and that it ends marked as a failure - and src/checkout.js is changed so that span is ended on the refusal branch. Delivering a refused-refund case that asserts only checkout.refund, or that works around the missing span in any way rather than fixing src/, scores zero for this criterion however green the suite is. Ending the span but leaving its status as it is set today scores at most half. Deleting the payments.refund span, or making the refund test cover only the successful path, scores zero.

support/trace-setup.js MUST NOT keep BatchSpanProcessor. Full marks require registering the processor that hands each ended span to the exporter in the caller's own tick, so a read straight after the exercised call sees the spans with no flush, no sleep and no timer left on the loop - and support/flush.js is no longer used by any test. Keeping BatchSpanProcessor and compensating with settleSpans(), a bare forceFlush, an awaited delay or a lowered scheduledDelayMillis scores zero here however green and however fast the suite ends up. Swapping the processor but leaving settleSpans() or any sleep in a test body scores at most half.

In test/cart.trace.test.js the `if (spans.length === 0) return;` early exit and the 200ms sleep are both gone, and the test now fails if cart.add emits no span. Leaving the early exit in place scores zero. Removing the sleep while keeping any construct that lets an empty read pass scores zero as well.

The declined-card case asserts the error status that src/checkout.js sets on both checkout.submit and payments.charge, and asserts payments.charge carries the outgoing-call span kind rather than the default in-process one. Asserting only span names and attributes, with no status and no kind, scores at most half.

New assertions resolve spans through a name lookup, the way the existing case does, rather than indexing spans[0]/spans[1] or relying on the order in which spans ended. Any positional index into the finished-span array in the new cases scores zero for this criterion.

The exporter is emptied between tests - a beforeEach or afterEach hook calling reset() - so the refund case does not read the checkout case's spans. Nothing in the shipped file trips over the leakage, so its absence is silent: no reset anywhere scores zero. A reset written inline in one test body only, leaving the ordering dependency for whoever adds the next case, scores at most half.

MUST NOT present raising `timeout-minutes` in .github/workflows/trace-tests.yml, or inserting an awaited delay before reading spans, as the fix for the wall clock. Doing either scores zero. Saying that the 2026-09-02 bump was treating a symptom and can now be put back earns full marks.

test/checkout.trace.test.js gains a declined-card case and a refused-refund case, and `npm test` passes with every pre-existing test still present. A missing case, a deleted test, or a red suite scores zero for this criterion.
vendor/tracing-sdk.js MUST NOT be modified - in particular its default scheduledDelayMillis MUST NOT be lowered to make the existing wiring look synchronous. Any edit to that file scores zero here.
docs/trace-test-setup.md exists, is ten lines or fewer, and names the change made to the shared wiring rather than restating the ticket.
